answer_text:
Let

\[
B_L=\left\{(x,y):\sqrt{(x-7)^2+(y+3)^2}<L\right\}.
\]

We need the largest \(L\) such that \(G\) is invertible on \(B_L\), i.e. one-to-one there (with smooth inverse, since \(G\) is smooth).

---

### 1. Check \(L=3\)

If \((x,y)\in B_3\), then

\[
|x-7|<3,\qquad |y+3|<3.
\]

Thus

\[
4<x<10,\qquad -6<y<0.
\]

So on \(B_3\),

\[
x-1>0,\qquad y<0.
\]

Now suppose

\[
G(x,y)=G(u,v)
\]

for two points \((x,y),(u,v)\in B_3\). Then

\[
(x-1)^2=(u-1)^2.
\]

Since \(x-1>0\) and \(u-1>0\), this forces

\[
x-1=u-1 \implies x=u.
\]

Also,

\[
y^4=v^4.
\]

Since \(y<0\) and \(v<0\), this forces

\[
y=v.
\]

Hence \(G\) is one-to-one on \(B_3\).

Moreover,

\[
DG(x,y)=
\begin{pmatrix}
2(x-1) & 0\\
0 & 4y^3
\end{pmatrix},
\]

so

\[
\det DG(x,y)=8(x-1)y^3\neq 0
\]

on \(B_3\). Therefore \(G\) is locally invertible everywhere in \(B_3\), and since it is one-to-one there, it is invertible on \(B_3\).

So \(L=3\) works.

---

### 2. Show no \(L>3\) works

Let \(L>3\). Choose \(\varepsilon>0\) such that

\[
0<\varepsilon<\min(3,L-3).
\]

Consider the two distinct points

\[
p=(7,\varepsilon),\qquad q=(7,-\varepsilon).
\]

Their distances from \((7,-3)\) are

\[
\|p-(7,-3)\|=3+\varepsilon<L,
\]

and

\[
\|q-(7,-3)\|=3-\varepsilon<3<L.
\]

Thus both \(p\) and \(q\) lie in \(B_L\). But

\[
G(p)=((7-1)^2,\varepsilon^4)=(36,\varepsilon^4),
\]

while

\[
G(q)=((7-1)^2,(-\varepsilon)^4)=(36,\varepsilon^4).
\]

So \(G(p)=G(q)\) with \(p\neq q\). Hence \(G\) is not one-to-one on \(B_L\), so it cannot be invertible there.

---

Therefore the largest possible radius is

\[
\boxed{3}
\]
